Excited to share that our paper “Programmable Quantum Matter: Heralding Large Cluster States in Driven Inhomogeneous Spin Ensembles” is now on arXiv: https://lnkd.in/e9R2uHqx One of the biggest challenges in scaling quantum systems at low temperatures (10 mK–1 K) is heat-induced decoherence. When control pulses arrive faster than the thermalization timescale of qubit’s local environment, local temperature rises and coherence is lost — directly limiting how many qubits can be operated simultaneously. In this work, we introduce a framework that turns a supposed weakness — inhomogeneities in spin ensembles (SiV color centers) — into a resource. Using global control, phase denoising, thermal modeling, and a modified single-photon entanglement protocol, we show how large entangled cluster states can be generated efficiently. An interesting coincidence is that, this project began 1.5 years ago, inspired by Dirk’s cantilever-based idea posted below, and only few months back did we discover that the term “Programmable Matter” was first introduced here at MIT 35 years ago by Prof. Tommaso Toffoli and Prof. Norman Margolus — in the context of cellular automata based multiprocessors. There’s a deep connection between cellular automata and entangled cluster states too… but that’s for the next time. Grateful to Prof. Dirk Englund for this opportunity and to my amazing colleagues Louis Follet and Odiel Hooybergs . More to come from MIT Quantum Photonics Laboratory 🚀 #QuantumComputing #Quantum #ClusterStates

🤔 What if the imperfections in quantum materials could actually become their greatest strength? ➡️ In our new work on '𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐦𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐦 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫: 𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐋𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞 𝐂𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐡𝐨𝐦𝐨𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐒𝐩𝐢𝐧 𝐄𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬' we show how the inhomogeneity of solid-state spin ensembles - often seen as a limitation - can be turned into a powerful resource: ✨ With global strain drive pulses (optimized via SAFE-GRAPE), we dynamically decouple all color centers at once, despite the inhomogeneity. ✨ We harness their spectral distinguishability to generate large entangled cluster states, a key building block for scalable quantum networks and measurement-based quantum computing. ✨ Our approach also lowers the cryogenic heating, making it possible to maintain spin coherence for longer and scale to larger systems. ❗Check out the full theoretical framework in our preprint: https://lnkd.in/erKM5get It was my pleasure to work on this theoretical concept together with Pratyush Anand and Louis Follet . Special thanks to Dirk Englund for sparking the idea and mentoring us throughout the project. I am grateful for a very interesting time as visiting researcher at MIT Quantum Photonics Laboratory and am happy we can finally share what we've been up to 🤗

As my time at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology came to a close last week, I am looking back with deep gratitude for the people and experiences that made this past year so special. During my time at MIT, I had the privilege of working in the MIT QP&AI Group . My research focused on interfacing with and controlling photonic integrated circuits (SiN) for the local addressing of tweezer-trapped rubidium atomic qubits. I want to express a sincere thank you to Prof. Dirk Englund and Dr. Adrian Menssen for the opportunity to work in the lab, as well as to my lab mates Thomas , Benjamin , and Hidde . Thank you all for your guidance, your support, and for making my time in the lab such a formative and enjoyable experience. I learned a lot from you all. Beyond the academic work, I also want to thank the MIT VISTA community. Thank you for welcoming me and for creating such a fantastic, supportive environment outside the lab. You made my time in Cambridge truly memorable. I’m very thankful for everyone who was part of this journey! #MIT #QuantumPhotonics #IntegratedPhotonics #QuantumComputing

How tightly should quantum processors and classical HPC be integrated? Until now, the answer has mostly been intuition. To address this, our team across NVIDIA , Amazon Web Services (AWS) , Berkeley Lab , and NASA Ames Research Center published a performance model that makes it quantitative, giving system builders and algorithm developers a concrete diagnostic to determine when co-location pays off, and when standard network connectivity is fine. Read the paper: https://bit.ly/3Re8t6x Huge thanks to my co-authors at NV ( Elica (Elitsa) Kyoseva , Jérôme Gonthier , Taylor Patti , Yuri Alexeev , Sam McArdle , Justin Lietz , Krysta Svore ), AWS( Dimitar Trenev , Sebastian Stern , Tyler Takeshita , Cedric Lin , Péter Kómár ), NERSC ( Katie Klymko , Ermal Rrapaj ) and NASA (Norm Tubman) for the fantastic work bringing this together, with special shout out to Elica (Elitsa) Kyoseva (NVIDIA) for supervising this work!

Excited to see this new work from our team at NVIDIA and collaborators at Amazon Web Services (AWS) , Berkeley Lab , and NASA Ames Research Center now available on arXiv: https://lnkd.in/eTCUgzdC Hybrid quantum-classical systems are often discussed in terms of integration, but until now we've lacked a performance model for understanding integration requirements quantitatively. By separating quantum compute, classical compute, and communication costs, this new framework helps determine when communication latency dominates, when computation dominates, and how those tradeoffs differ between application-level workflows and real-time workloads such as calibration, control, and decoding for quantum error correction. The ability to quantify these requirements is important not only for designing today's systems, but also for identifying how integration requirements may evolve as quantum hardware, algorithms, and classical computing continue to advance. Many thanks and congratulations to Pooja Rao and the broader collaborative team for driving this work forward! 🎉 Happy to share that we will be presenting our work on explainable AI and the challenge of measuring feature importance when models disagree at the International Conference on Machine Learning ( #ICML 2026). This is joint work with Ángel David Reyero Lobo , Denis A. Engemann , and Bertrand Thirion . 🎯 Explainable AI promises to reveal what complex models, often considered black boxes, learn during training, thereby increasing trust in their predictions. For instance, explaining a model trained to predict disease risk from large clinical cohorts can help identify new risk factors and ways to prevent disease. ⚠️ However, complex AI models are prone to instability, making them hard to interpret; small perturbations in training can change the inner workings of these models. This phenomenon is known as the Rashomon effect. It was named after a movie depicting conflicting witness accounts of the same incident during a trial. 💡 We study how best to mitigate this effect. Should we aggregate the explanations of multiple models, or explain a single larger model that itself aggregates predictions? Our analysis reveals that the second approach is more effective, providing practitioners with a simple guideline for obtaining more reliable explanations from complex models. 🎬 To pursue the analogy: should multiple juries each hear one witness and then aggregate their verdicts, or should a single jury hear all witnesses and deliver one verdict? link: https://lnkd.in/ePJBH3sy pdf: https://lnkd.in/eP9a4YPh
